page: Microsoft Azure HB120-32rs_v3 is an instance within the High Performance Computing family, provisioned through the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. The system allocates 32 dedicated vCPUs built on an x86_64 architecture Intel processor. Total system memory measures 456.0 GB, yielding a high memory density of 14.25 GB of RAM per core. This memory-to-core ratio allows memory-constrained execution threads to access substantial headroom without resource contention.

Local I/O performance is backed by an integrated 2,435 GB NVMe solid-state drive, complemented by support for Premium Storage volumes. Network interconnects are RDMA capable, facilitating low-latency communication across node clusters. The instance profile does not include discrete GPU accelerators and provides zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses, requiring standard cloud networking mechanisms for external routing.

By constraining the core count to 32 dedicated vCPUs while retaining access to the platform's 456.0 GB memory footprint, the instance offers favorable resource density for software environments governed by per-core software licensing models. This hardware profile is appropriate for memory-bound high-performance computing workloads, large in-memory databases, scientific simulations, and data-intensive analytics tasks.
description: Microsoft Azure HB120-32rs_v3 is a High Performance Computing instance built on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features 32 dedicated vCPUs on an x86_64 architecture Intel processor paired with 456.0 GB of memory, yielding 14.25 GB of RAM per vCPU core. Storage is provisioned via an integrated 2,435 GB local NVMe SSD alongside support for Premium Storage tiers. The instance incorporates RDMA network capabilities for low-latency cluster communication, while omitting discrete GPUs and complimentary public IPv4 addresses. With its high memory-per-core allocation and fast local NVMe storage, this configuration optimizes cost efficiency for applications constrained by per-core software licensing or significant RAM requirements rather than absolute core counts. It is well matched for memory-intensive high-performance computing tasks, large-scale data analytics, in-memory databases, and scientific simulations requiring rapid local scratch space and high memory bandwidth per execution thread.
